messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: taking away correlations results in
parts:
The first commented-out line allows residual covariance between the two observed variable loading on a common factor. Yes, those variables should covary because they are jointly dependent on a common factor, but the covariance of these two observed variables is important for estimating model parameters in the constrained model. If you allow the residual covariance as wel, then this information must be used for that purpose and is not available for estimating other parameters. That creates an identification problem--no unique solution for the model. Leaving out that line does not mean that the two variables are orthogonal--it just measn that the factor model accounts for their covariance, leaving nothing left over.

The proportionately large difference between the original and robust chi-squares indicates a distribution that is relatively far from normal. Since the robust chi-square is larger (the robust is most typically smaller), this suggests to me that your data distribution is platykurtic or flat (with thin tails) relative to the normal distribution.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: taking away correlations results in
parts:
If a variable is dependent on another variable (and that includes observed variables loading on a common factor), then the ~~ operator refers to residual covariance, not total covariance. Using the ~~ operator with a dependent variable means that the rest of the model is NOT sufficient to account for the total covariance between the variables. Using the ~~ operator relaxes a constraint on covariances, unless you specify:
varA ~~ 0*varB
which constrains the covariance, or the residual covariance, to 0.
     Well, if your data distribution is a surprise, then maybe you should inspect your data for typos or outliers. Use histobgrams and scatterplots to visually inspect for unusual values. Particularly in a small dataset, one or two extreme values can have a major impact. If you know that the distribution is nonnormal, you will want to rely on the robust estimators.
     If you are using the lavaan::sem function, then residual variances for single indicators are fixed to 0 by default. If this had not been done, then your model would have failed identification for this reason, as well. If you switch to the lavaan::lavaan function, this default would no longer be in place, and you would see the consequences. If you want to set these residual variances to something other than 0, you will need to use syntax for that. To set the residual variance of varA to 0.2:
varA~~0.2*varA
